meta.name: Health
meta.about: Health and wellness topics explained through the anatomy and physiology they act on. Guidance follows WHO, NHS and UK Chief Medical Officers' recommendations. Educational; not a personal plan.

exercise.name: Exercise and physical activity
exercise.summary: Movement is the single intervention that improves almost every organ system at once: it strengthens the heart, lowers blood pressure and blood sugar, builds muscle and bone, lifts mood and sleep, and cuts the risk of the commonest causes of death by a quarter or more.
body: Aerobic activity (walking, cycling, swimming, running) trains the heart to pump more per beat, so resting heart rate falls and the same effort costs less. Capillaries multiply in muscle, mitochondria increase, and the muscles' ability to take up glucose without insulin improves within a single session, which is why activity is a treatment for type 2 diabetes.

Strength training loads muscle and bone. Muscle fibres thicken in response to progressive overload; bone responds to impact and pulling by laying down more mineral, the only lifestyle measure that reliably builds bone density. After the age of 30, adults lose 3-8% of muscle mass per decade unless they resist it, and that loss drives falls, frailty and loss of independence in old age.

Activity also acts on the brain: it raises BDNF and blood flow to the hippocampus, improves memory and attention, is as effective as medication for mild to moderate depression, and lowers dementia risk. Sitting for long periods is a risk factor independent of exercise, so breaking up sitting matters too.

effects.effect: Lower resting heart rate and blood pressure, higher stroke volume, better coronary blood flow; 20-35% lower risk of coronary disease
Improved insulin sensitivity, lower HbA1c, 30-40% lower risk of type 2 diabetes
Hypertrophy and strength; preserved mass and function with age
Higher bone density and lower fracture risk with weight-bearing and resistance exercise
Better mood, sleep and cognition; lower risk of depression and dementia
Lower risk of bowel, breast and other cancers, partly via weight, insulin and inflammation

guidance: Adults: at least 150 minutes of moderate activity (brisk walking, where you can talk but not sing) or 75 minutes of vigorous activity per week, spread across the week
Muscle-strengthening activity on at least 2 days a week, working all major groups
Over 65: add balance and strength work (tai chi, dancing, stairs) to reduce falls
Minimise long periods of sitting; any movement is better than none, and benefits start well below the target
Children 5-17: 60 minutes a day, including vigorous and bone-strengthening activity

sleep.name: Sleep
sleep.summary: Sleep is not downtime: the brain clears metabolic waste, consolidates memory and resets emotional circuits, while the body repairs tissue, releases growth hormone and regulates appetite and immune hormones. Adults need seven to nine hours, and chronic short sleep raises the risk of obesity, diabetes, heart disease, depression and accidents.
body: Sleep cycles through light sleep, deep slow-wave sleep and REM sleep roughly every 90 minutes. Deep sleep dominates early in the night: heart rate and blood pressure fall, growth hormone is released, and the glymphatic system flushes cerebrospinal fluid through the brain, clearing amyloid and other waste. REM sleep dominates later, when the brain replays and files the day's experiences and dreams occur while the body is paralysed.

Timing is set by the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, a clock synchronised to light reaching the retina. Melatonin from the pineal gland rises in darkness and signals night. Evening light from screens delays the clock; morning daylight advances it, which is why light exposure is the most powerful lever for shifting sleep.

Sleep pressure builds through the day as adenosine accumulates; caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors, with a half-life of five to six hours. Alcohol induces sleep but fragments it and suppresses REM. Obstructive sleep apnoea, where the throat closes repeatedly, causes loud snoring, witnessed pauses and daytime sleepiness, and raises blood pressure and heart risk.

effects.effect: Memory consolidation, emotional regulation, waste clearance; short sleep impairs attention like alcohol
Growth hormone release; short sleep raises cortisol and ghrelin (hunger) and lowers leptin and insulin sensitivity
Nightly dip in blood pressure; chronic short sleep and apnoea raise blood pressure and coronary risk
Immune memory formed during sleep; vaccine responses and infection resistance fall with sleep loss

guidance: Adults 7-9 hours; teenagers 8-10; young children 10-13
Keep a regular wake time, including weekends; get daylight within an hour of waking
Dim lights and avoid screens in the hour before bed; keep the bedroom cool, dark and quiet
No caffeine after early afternoon; avoid alcohol and large meals close to bedtime
Reserve the bed for sleep: if awake for more than 20 minutes, get up and do something quiet until sleepy
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the first-line treatment, ahead of sleeping tablets; loud snoring with pauses or daytime sleepiness needs assessment for apnoea

nutrition.name: Nutrition
nutrition.summary: Food supplies energy, the building blocks for every tissue, and the vitamins and minerals that enzymes need. The pattern that best protects the heart, brain and gut across large studies is built on vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts, fish and olive oil, with little processed meat, refined sugar and salt.
body: Carbohydrates are broken down to glucose in the small intestine and absorbed into the portal vein to the liver; fibre is the part that reaches the colon undigested, where bacteria ferment it to short-chain fatty acids that feed the bowel lining, lower inflammation and help regulate appetite. Whole grains, beans and vegetables deliver glucose slowly; refined sugar and white flour deliver it in a surge that demands more insulin.

Protein provides amino acids for muscle, enzymes, hormones and immune cells; adults need about 0.75-1 g per kilogram a day, more when older or training. Fats build cell membranes and carry vitamins A, D, E and K: unsaturated fats from olive oil, nuts and oily fish lower LDL cholesterol, while saturated and especially industrial trans fats raise it.

Salt draws water into the blood and raises blood pressure: most adults eat 8-9 g a day against a 5-6 g limit, three-quarters of it hidden in bread, processed meat and ready meals. Micronutrients matter in specific ways: iron for haemoglobin, calcium and vitamin D for bone, folate before and during pregnancy, B12 for nerves (a risk on vegan diets and with metformin), iodine for the thyroid.

effects.effect: Fibre feeds the microbiome, prevents constipation, lowers bowel cancer risk by about 10% per 10 g a day
Unsaturated fats and fibre lower LDL; salt reduction lowers blood pressure; Mediterranean diet cuts cardiovascular events by about 30%
Slow-release carbohydrate and healthy weight prevent and can reverse type 2 diabetes
Calcium, vitamin D and protein maintain bone; vitamin D deficiency is common in northern winters
Mediterranean-style eating is linked to slower cognitive decline and lower depression risk

guidance: At least 5 portions of fruit and vegetables a day (400 g), varied in colour
Base meals on whole grains and legumes; aim for 30 g of fibre a day
Two portions of fish a week, one oily; limit red meat to about 70 g a day and avoid processed meat
Salt under 6 g (2.4 g sodium) a day; free sugars under 30 g a day (about 7 teaspoons); sugary drinks are the easiest cut
Choose unsaturated oils and spreads; keep saturated fat under 10% of energy
Vitamin D 10 micrograms daily in autumn and winter in northern latitudes; folic acid 400 micrograms when planning pregnancy

weight.name: Body weight
weight.summary: Body fat is an active endocrine organ. Excess fat, particularly around the abdominal organs, releases inflammatory signals and free fatty acids that make tissues resistant to insulin, raise blood pressure and cholesterol, load the joints and narrow the airway in sleep. Losing 5-10% of body weight measurably improves all of these.
body: Energy balance is regulated by the hypothalamus, which reads leptin from fat stores, insulin, and gut hormones such as ghrelin (hunger, from the stomach) and GLP-1 (fullness, from the small intestine). Modern food environments overwhelm these signals with energy-dense, highly palatable food and reduced movement; genetics sets how strongly each person's appetite responds. Weight is therefore not simply willpower, and biology fights weight loss by increasing hunger and lowering energy expenditure.

Where fat sits matters more than how much. Visceral fat packed around the liver, pancreas and intestines drains straight into the portal vein and drives fatty liver, insulin resistance and inflammation; fat under the skin of the hips is metabolically quieter. Waist circumference above 94 cm in men or 80 cm in women marks raised risk, and BMI thresholds are lower in South Asian and some other populations.

Weight loss of 5-10% reduces blood pressure, HbA1c and liver fat, eases knee pain and sleep apnoea, and a 15 kg loss can put type 2 diabetes into remission in about half of people within six years of diagnosis. Sustainable approaches combine reduced energy intake, protein and fibre to preserve fullness, resistance exercise to keep muscle, sleep and behavioural support; GLP-1 medicines and bariatric surgery act on the same hormone pathways for those with obesity-related disease.

effects.effect: Insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome; reversed in part by weight loss
Higher blood pressure and LDL, more coronary disease and stroke
Each kilogram of body weight adds about 4 kg of load across the knee when walking; osteoarthritis risk rises steeply
Fatty liver disease (now the commonest liver condition), gallstones, reflux, and higher risk of bowel, liver and oesophageal cancer
Obstructive sleep apnoea and breathlessness from reduced lung volumes

guidance: Know your numbers: BMI (weight in kg divided by height in m squared; 25-30 overweight, over 30 obesity, lower cut-offs of 23 and 27.5 for South Asian, Chinese, Black African and Middle Eastern backgrounds) and waist circumference
Aim first for 5-10% loss over 3-6 months, about 0.5-1 kg a week, through a sustained energy deficit of around 600 kcal a day
Prioritise protein, vegetables and fibre; cut sugary drinks, alcohol and ultra-processed snacks; keep regular meals
Combine with 150 minutes of activity and twice-weekly strength work to protect muscle; sleep 7-9 hours
Seek structured support (group programmes, dietitian); medication or surgery are options for obesity with related disease, prescribed and monitored by specialists

smoking.name: Smoking and vaping
smoking.summary: Tobacco smoke delivers nicotine, an addictive stimulant, in a cloud of 7,000 chemicals including 70 known carcinogens, carbon monoxide and tar. It damages every organ it reaches: it is the leading preventable cause of cancer, heart disease and lung disease, and kills half of long-term users. Stopping at any age recovers much of the risk, and the fall begins within hours.
body: In the lungs, hot smoke paralyses and then destroys the cilia that sweep mucus and microbes out of the airways, inflames the bronchi (chronic bronchitis), and the enzymes released by inflammatory cells digest the walls of the alveoli (emphysema), so gas exchange fails. Tar coats the lining and its carcinogens mutate the DNA of bronchial cells: lung cancer risk is 15-30 times that of a never-smoker, and cancers of the mouth, throat, oesophagus, bladder, pancreas, kidney, stomach, cervix and bowel are all increased.

Carbon monoxide occupies haemoglobin, cutting oxygen delivery; nicotine drives adrenaline, raising heart rate and blood pressure; and the chemicals injure the endothelium lining every artery, letting cholesterol enter the wall and making blood stickier. The result is atherosclerosis in the coronary, carotid, cerebral and leg arteries, doubling heart attack and stroke risk and causing most cases of peripheral arterial disease and aortic aneurysm.

Nicotine reaches the brain in ten seconds and releases dopamine in the reward pathway; receptors multiply, so the brain demands nicotine to feel normal and withdrawal brings irritability, restlessness and craving. That biology, not weakness, is why stopping is hard and why nicotine replacement, varenicline and behavioural support together triple the chance of success. E-cigarettes deliver nicotine without combustion and are substantially less harmful than smoking, which makes them a useful quitting tool for smokers, but they are not harmless and are not for non-smokers or young people.

effects.effect: COPD (smoking causes 9 in 10 cases), lung cancer, pneumonia, worse asthma; passive smoke causes the same diseases in others
Atherosclerosis: heart attack, stroke, aneurysm, peripheral arterial disease, erectile dysfunction
Cancers of the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, bowel; peptic ulcers; Crohn disease flares
Bladder and kidney cancer; faster decline in kidney disease
Osteoporosis, slower fracture and wound healing
Reduced fertility, miscarriage, stillbirth, low birth weight, sudden infant death

guidance: There is no safe level of smoking; stopping completely is the goal, and the benefits start within a day (carbon monoxide gone), weeks (breathing and circulation improve), a year (heart attack risk halved) and a decade (lung cancer risk halved)
Use support: stop-smoking services, nicotine replacement (patch plus a fast-acting form), varenicline or cytisine, or switching fully to vaping
Set a quit date, remove tobacco and lighters, plan for triggers, and treat a lapse as a lesson rather than a failure
Keep homes and cars smoke-free to protect children
Smokers aged 55-74 are offered lung cancer screening with low-dose CT in a growing number of countries

alcohol.name: Alcohol
alcohol.summary: Alcohol is absorbed from the stomach and small intestine, distributed through body water and processed by the liver at roughly one unit an hour. In the short term it depresses the brain; over years it damages the liver, heart, pancreas, nerves and brain and causes seven types of cancer. Risk rises with every drink; there is no fully safe level, but keeping under 14 units a week spread over several days keeps it low.
body: The liver converts alcohol to acetaldehyde, a toxic carcinogen, and then to acetate. Fat accumulates in liver cells within days of heavy drinking (fatty liver, reversible with abstinence); continued drinking inflames the liver (alcoholic hepatitis) and scars it (cirrhosis), which blocks blood flow from the gut, backs pressure into oesophageal veins that can bleed, and destroys the liver's ability to make proteins and clear toxins.

In the brain, alcohol enhances GABA inhibition and blocks glutamate: judgement, coordination and memory fail in proportion to the blood level, and at high levels breathing and gag reflexes are suppressed, which is how binge drinking kills. Regular use makes the brain adapt, so stopping suddenly causes rebound overactivity: tremor, seizures and delirium tremens, which can be fatal without medical withdrawal. Thiamine deficiency in heavy drinkers damages the memory circuits (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome).

Alcohol raises blood pressure, causes atrial fibrillation ('holiday heart') and weakens the heart muscle (cardiomyopathy); it inflames the pancreas and the stomach lining; and acetaldehyde plus its effect on oestrogen and folate causes cancers of the mouth, throat, oesophagus, liver, bowel and breast. Its calories (7 kcal per gram) contribute to weight gain, and it disrupts sleep architecture even in moderate amounts.

effects.effect: Fatty liver, hepatitis, cirrhosis; pancreatitis; gastritis and ulcers; cancers of the mouth to bowel
Intoxication, blackouts, dependence, withdrawal seizures, peripheral neuropathy, dementia, depression
Hypertension, atrial fibrillation, cardiomyopathy, stroke
Low blood sugar in binges, raised triglycerides, gout, reduced testosterone
Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder: no safe amount in pregnancy

guidance: No more than 14 units a week for both men and women, spread over 3 or more days, with several drink-free days; a unit is 10 mL of pure alcohol, roughly half a pint of ordinary beer, a small (125 mL) glass of wine, or a single 25 mL measure of spirits
Avoid binges (more than 6 units in one session); eat before drinking and alternate with water
None in pregnancy or when planning one; none before driving, operating machinery or swimming

Warning signs of dependence: needing a drink to start the day, shaking when stopping, drinking more than intended, others expressing concern; anyone drinking heavily every day should not stop abruptly without medical advice
Liver tests, blood pressure and support services (talking therapies, medication such as acamprosate or naltrexone) are available through primary care

hydration.name: Hydration
hydration.summary: Water makes up about 60% of an adult's body and is the medium for every chemical reaction, the carrier for every nutrient and waste product, and the body's coolant. The kidneys and the thirst centre match intake to loss with remarkable precision; problems arise at the extremes: dehydration in heat, illness and old age, and, more rarely, drinking so much that sodium is diluted.
body: Water leaves the body as urine (about 1.5 litres a day), sweat, water vapour in breath and a little in stool: roughly 2-2.5 litres in temperate conditions, far more in heat or exercise. About 20% of intake comes from food; the rest from drinks of any kind, since tea, coffee and milk count. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a rise in blood concentration of as little as 1-2% and trigger thirst and the release of antidiuretic hormone, which tells the kidney's collecting ducts to reabsorb water and concentrate the urine.

Mild dehydration (1-2% of body weight) causes thirst, dark urine, headache, tiredness and poorer concentration; moderate dehydration lowers blood pressure, speeds the heart and reduces urine output; severe dehydration causes confusion, kidney injury and collapse. Older people feel thirst less and have less kidney reserve, babies lose water fast through their large surface area and vomiting or diarrhoea, and both need watching in hot weather and illness.

Overdrinking is the rarer danger: drinking several litres in a short time, particularly during endurance events or with some psychiatric conditions and drugs, dilutes blood sodium (hyponatraemia), swelling brain cells and causing headache, confusion, seizures and death. Sports drinks with electrolytes are needed only for sustained exercise over about an hour; for everyone else, water is the right drink, and sugary drinks are the ones to cut.

effects.effect: Adequate intake dilutes urine and halves the recurrence of kidney stones; concentrated urine irritates the bladder and favours infection
Dehydration impairs concentration, mood and reaction time and triggers headaches and migraine
Low volume drops blood pressure and causes dizziness on standing, especially with diuretics and in the elderly
Fluid keeps stool soft; constipation worsens with dehydration
Sweating is the main heat loss mechanism and fails without water; heat illness follows

guidance: Around 6-8 glasses (1.5-2 litres) of fluid a day for most adults, more in heat, exercise, fever, vomiting or diarrhoea, pregnancy and breastfeeding
Use urine colour as the guide: pale straw is right, dark yellow means drink more; thirst is a late signal in older people
Water, lower-fat milk and unsweetened tea or coffee are the best choices; limit fruit juice and smoothies to 150 mL a day and avoid sugary drinks

In illness with vomiting or diarrhoea, small frequent sips of oral rehydration solution replace salts as well as water; seek help for a baby or older person who is not passing urine, is drowsy or has sunken eyes
During prolonged exercise drink to thirst and include sodium; do not force fluids beyond that

transgender-health.name: Transgender and non-binary health
transgender-health.summary: Trans and non-binary people need the same care as everyone else plus a few things specific to their bodies and treatment: monitoring of gender-affirming hormones, screening matched to the organs they have rather than the gender on their record, attention to bone, clot and cardiovascular risk, fertility and sexual health, and mental health support against the effects of stigma. The organising principle is simple: care follows anatomy.
body: WPATH, the Endocrine Society and the UCSF Gender Affirming Health Program set out how to care for trans women, trans men and non-binary people. Gender incongruence is classified by the World Health Organization under conditions related to sexual health, not as a mental disorder. Much of good care is ordinary general practice done respectfully: the person's name and pronouns, an accurate record of the organs they have, and hormone therapy monitored like any other long-term medicine. Referral to an NHS gender identity service is made by a GP and waiting times are long, so general practice usually holds the person's ongoing care, often under a shared care agreement, while they wait. Screening invitations and some laboratory reference ranges follow the gender marker on the record rather than the body, so a trans man registered as male is not invited for cervical screening. An inventory of the organs present, updated after surgery, is the practical fix.

Feminising therapy is oestradiol, by patch, gel, tablet or injection, with a testosterone-suppressing medicine until the testes are removed; masculinising therapy is testosterone by gel or injection. Guidelines set the monitoring: hormone levels, aiming for the range of the affirmed gender; potassium and kidney function on spironolactone; haemoglobin and haematocrit on testosterone; blood pressure, weight, lipids, glucose and liver function on both; and prolactin if symptoms such as galactorrhoea, headache or visual change suggest a raised level (guidelines differ on routine testing). Oestrogen raises the risk of venous thrombosis, most with oral preparations, smoking and immobility, so transdermal routes are preferred for people at higher risk. Both hormones protect bone, so bone density is assessed after gonadectomy if hormones are stopped or levels stay low. Both regimens reduce fertility, and storing sperm or eggs is offered before starting.

Screening follows the organs present. Anyone with a cervix, including trans men and non-binary people, needs cervical screening from 25 and may have to ask for it; a trans woman has no cervix and does not. Testosterone thins the cervical and vaginal lining, so the test can be uncomfortable and samples are more often reported as inadequate; noting testosterone use on the request form, a smaller speculum, lubricant, or a short course of vaginal oestrogen before the test all help. Trans women registered as female are invited for breast screening between 50 and 71; those registered as male are not invited and can ask for it. The risk that screening addresses follows years of feminising hormones, so invitation depends on the register while the reason for screening depends on hormone exposure. Breast tissue develops on oestrogen, and the breast cancer risk of trans women on long-term oestrogen is thought to be higher than that of cis men though lower than that of cis women. Chest masculinisation leaves some breast tissue, so a new lump still needs assessment. The prostate is not removed at vaginoplasty: it lies behind the front wall of the neovagina, can be examined through it, and PSA is interpreted knowing that testosterone suppression lowers it. Bowel screening is offered by age to everyone in the eligible range whatever the gender marker on the record, and abdominal aortic aneurysm screening is offered to men at 65, so a trans woman registered as female is not invited automatically and can ask.

Testosterone is not contraception: ovulation can continue after periods stop, and testosterone is stopped before a planned pregnancy. Feminising therapy lowers sperm production but is not reliable contraception either. Condoms, regular testing for sexually transmitted infections and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) where appropriate apply as to anyone; a skin-lined neovagina does not self-lubricate and needs lubricant and regular dilation. After phalloplasty, difficulty passing urine, spraying, leaking or repeated urinary infection should be reported, because urethral stricture and fistula are the commonest complications. Chest binding is safer with a purpose-made binder rather than bandages or tape, with breaks in the day and none overnight, and the same caution applies to tucking. Trans people experience more depression, anxiety and self-harm than the general population, driven largely by rejection, discrimination and delays in care rather than by being trans; support and affirming care reduce that risk, and urgent help is available for anyone thinking of suicide.

effects.effect: Hormone therapy shifts oestradiol and testosterone into the range of the affirmed gender; levels, potassium and kidney function on spironolactone, lipids and glucose are monitored
Fertility falls on both regimens; retained organs (the prostate in trans women; the cervix, uterus and ovaries in trans men unless removed) keep their own risks and screening
Sex hormones protect bone; density can fall after gonadectomy or when hormones are interrupted, so bone health is assessed
Blood pressure, weight, lipids and glucose are checked at reviews because both regimens alter cardiovascular risk factors, and smoking adds to the risk
Oestrogen softens skin and slows hair growth; testosterone brings acne, oilier skin and male-pattern hair; hair removal and acne care are common needs
Oestrogen raises the risk of venous thromboembolism, most with oral preparations, smoking and immobility; testosterone raises haematocrit

guidance: Tell your GP and any clinic which organs you have, including after surgery, so that screening, tests and reference ranges follow your anatomy rather than the gender marker on your record

Screening follows your anatomy: anyone with a cervix, including trans men and non-binary people, needs cervical screening from 25 and should ask if not invited; trans women should attend breast screening when invited or ask for it if registered as male; trans men who have not had chest surgery should ask to be screened if not invited, and after chest surgery any new lump still needs assessment
Trans women keep a prostate: report urinary symptoms, and ask about abdominal aortic aneurysm screening at 65 if not invited
Attend hormone monitoring (blood tests, blood pressure, weight) and do not take hormones bought online without telling a doctor, so that levels and blood counts can be checked

Do not smoke: smoking multiplies the clot risk of oestrogen and the cardiovascular risk of either regimen; keep active and know the signs of a clot (swollen painful leg, chest pain, sudden breathlessness)

Discuss storing sperm or eggs before starting hormones or having surgery on the testes or ovaries; neither testosterone nor oestrogen is contraception, so use contraception if pregnancy is to be avoided, and use condoms and consider PrEP
Bind and tuck safely: a purpose-made binder, not bandages or tape, taken off to sleep and loosened for strenuous exercise; see a doctor for pain, breathlessness or skin damage
Ask for mental health support if low mood or anxiety persist, and get urgent help from emergency services or a crisis line for thoughts of suicide or self-harm

womens-health.name: Women's health through the life course
womens-health.summary: Women's health covers the care of organs that change every month and at every stage of life: periods, contraception and fertility, pregnancy, the menopause, the pelvic floor, screening for cervical, breast and bowel cancer, and illnesses that behave differently in women. Care follows anatomy, so trans men and non-binary people with these organs need the same care.
body: The menstrual cycle sets the rhythm of the reproductive years: cycles of about 21 to 35 days are typical, and the NHS counts regular cycles anywhere from 21 to 40 days as normal. Bleeding heavy enough to disrupt daily life, pain that ordinary painkillers do not control, and bleeding between periods, after sex or after the menopause are all worth reporting. Endometriosis, fibroids and polycystic ovary syndrome lie behind many such symptoms. Heavy periods are the commonest cause of iron deficiency anaemia before the menopause, so a full blood count and ferritin are checked when bleeding is heavy or tiredness persists.

Contraception works by stopping ovulation (the combined pill, patch, ring, implant and injection), by thickening cervical mucus and thinning the lining (progestogen-only pills and the hormonal coil, which also lightens heavy periods), by barrier (condoms, which also prevent sexually transmitted infections), or permanently by sterilisation. Before a planned pregnancy, folic acid is advised from before conception through the first 12 weeks, and smoking, alcohol, long-term conditions and regular medicines are reviewed. Antenatal care checks blood pressure and urine; afterwards the pelvic floor, mood and bleeding need attention.

The menopause is 12 months after the last period, on average around 51 in the UK, with the perimenopause running for years before it. Falling oestradiol brings hot flushes, night sweats, disturbed sleep, low mood, joint aches, vaginal dryness and urinary symptoms. Hormone replacement therapy relieves them, with a progestogen added for anyone who still has a uterus, and vaginal oestrogen treats local symptoms. Bone loss is fastest around the menopause and cardiovascular risk rises after it; chest pain is still the commonest sign of a heart attack in women, and accompanying breathlessness, nausea or pain in the jaw, back or arm are more often attributed to something else.

Cervical screening covers everyone with a cervix from 25 to 64 in England and tests first for high-risk HPV. Breast screening offers a mammogram every three years from 50 to 71; trans women are eligible after at least two years of feminising hormones, and trans men who have not had chest surgery remain eligible. Invitations follow the gender you are registered as with the GP, so anyone registered as male will need to ask rather than wait for a letter. Bowel screening posts a home kit for a faecal immunochemical test to those in the eligible age range. Screening is not a test for symptoms: a new lump, a nipple or skin change, or bleeding after the menopause needs prompt examination.

effects.effect: The cycle, fertility and pregnancy depend on the ovaries and uterus; endometriosis, fibroids and polycystic ovary syndrome are common causes of pain, heavy or irregular bleeding and difficulty conceiving
Oestradiol and progesterone rise and fall each month, climb steeply in pregnancy and fall at the menopause, and those shifts change bones, skin, sleep, mood and the vagina
Bone density peaks in early adult life and falls fastest in the years around the menopause, so osteoporosis and fragility fractures are commoner in women

Cardiovascular risk rises after the menopause; chest pain remains the commonest sign of a heart attack in women, and accompanying breathlessness, nausea or pain in the jaw, back or arm are more often attributed to other causes
Pregnancy, birth and the fall in oestrogen weaken pelvic support and thin the urethral lining, so urinary infections, stress incontinence and prolapse are common and treatable

The national programmes cover cervical, breast and bowel cancer; there is no screening test for ovarian or womb cancer, so persistent bloating, feeling full quickly, new pelvic pain or any bleeding after the menopause need assessment rather than waiting for a screening invitation

guidance: Know your own pattern and report change: bleeding heavy enough to disrupt daily life, pain that ordinary painkillers do not control, new irregularity, bleeding between periods or after sex, and any bleeding after the menopause
Attend cervical screening from 25 to 64; it is for everyone with a cervix, including trans men and non-binary people, who may need to ask for it if registered as male

Attend breast screening when invited, and ask for it rather than wait for a letter if you are registered as male: trans women are eligible after at least two years of feminising hormones, and trans men who have not had chest surgery remain eligible; get a new lump, skin dimpling, nipple change or blood-stained discharge checked promptly whatever the last mammogram showed

Choose contraception with a clinician rather than by reputation: methods differ in how they work, how they affect periods and what suits your health history, and emergency contraception works best the sooner it is used
Before a planned pregnancy take folic acid from before conception through the first 12 weeks, stop smoking, avoid alcohol, and have long-term conditions and regular medicines reviewed

Train the pelvic floor lifelong: squeeze as if stopping wind and the flow of urine, hold and release, several times a day, during and after pregnancy, and keep it up for at least three months before judging the benefit

Talk about menopausal symptoms rather than tolerating them, and get any bleeding after the menopause assessed urgently; hormone replacement therapy, with a progestogen if you have a uterus, and vaginal oestrogen are effective for most people; discuss the benefits and risks for you, including the type and route of oestrogen
Protect bone and heart from midlife onwards with weight-bearing and strength exercise, enough calcium and vitamin D, no smoking, moderate alcohol, and blood pressure and cholesterol checks
